messages.subject: Handling incomplete cases
messages.body_plain:
All,

I'm just getting started with occupancy modeling and have run into a road block I know I can fix... with some guidance.

What is the best way to handle incomplete cases? I have a dataset with some missing values for detection covariates where observers did not record all of the necessary information (e.g., start time of survey, or temperature) despite conducting a survey.

Error in msPGOcc(), : error: some elements in det.covs have missing values where there is an observed data value in y. Please either replace the NA values in det.covs with non-missing values (e.g., mean imputation) or set the corresponding values in y to NA where the covariate is missing.

These gaps do not perfectly overlap each other across all surveys, detection covariates, or detection histories. So far, I have only attempted working with Julian date and time of day as detection covariates. It strikes me that methods of filling missing data (e.g., mean imputation) would be inappropriate for these variables (maybe you have some other idea?). Any suggestions are much appreciated!

Sincerely,
Sam O'Dell

messages.subject: Recommended offset for spNMix with point-count (camera trap) data?
messages.subject_clean: Recommended offset for spNMix with point-count (camera trap) data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm running a simulation study to test how well spNMix recovers true total abundance (N) from simulated camera trap data, and I've hit a design question I'd appreciate some guidance on.

While setting up the simulation, I noticed that changing the offset value passed into data for spNMix() changes the resulting abundance predictions, which makes sense given how offset enters the abundance model (mu = offset * exp(Xβ)). I've put together a minimal reproducible example that isolates this and shows the effect clearly (attached).

My question is about what's recommended for offset in a design like mine. Most of the guidance and examples I've seen seem to assume a transect-based design, where offset maps naturally onto transect length or area surveyed. My cameras are stationary point counts rather than transects, so there's no natural "length" to use, and it's not obvious to me what the offset should represent instead — e.g., whether it should just be left at 1, represent some notion of the area covered by a single camera's detection zone, or be tied to the spacing/area of the camera grid itself.

Any guidance (or pointers to a relevant paper/example) on how offset should be handled for point-count camera trap designs specifically would be really helpful.

Thanks in advance,
Chrysanthe

messages.subject: Re: Handling incomplete cases
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sam,

Sorry for the delay in response. There is no single best way to handle situations like the one you describe where observers did not collect all the relevant detection covariates during a survey. There are of course limitations to any imputation approach, as it has the potential to bias results if the imputation is not accurate. Mean imputation is arguably the most simple approach, but you aren't necessary restricted to taking the mean across the whole data set and instead you could take the mean for a subset of the data that is perhaps more closely tied to the missing observation. For example, if there is a detection variable measured over time for repeated visits at a site and some of them are missing, you could take the mean of the variable when it is measured at the site to fill in the values for when it is missing. There are a variety of more advanced missing data imputation approaches, the most complex of which would seek to fit some model to the covariate that has missing data to try and predict the missing values, and then you would use those model-predicted values as inputs into the occupancy model. Some Google searches regarding missing data imputation approaches in ecology turns up a variety of useful references. This recent paper <https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecm.70037> by Mike Dumelle gives a broad overview of the statistical challenges with data imputation that could be of interest.

Jeff

messages.subject: Re: Recommended offset for spNMix with point-count (camera trap) data?
messages.subject_clean: Recommended offset for spNMix with point-count (camera trap) data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chrysanthe,

Thanks for the note. Quantifying the area that is sampled with a camera trap, or many other monitoring approaches (e.g., ARUs, traditional surveys), is not extremely straightforward, particularly when working with mobile species. The effective area sampled is likely to vary with different characteristics of the site (e.g., vegetation) and period of sampling (e.g., weather conditions). This general challenge of estimating the area sampled to scale some measure of relative abundance to density is discussed in the Applied Hierarchical Modeling Part 1 book by Marc Kéry and Andy Royle, although I can't remember the specific section number off the top of my head. I think this concept was also discussed in a review <https://conbio.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/cobi.13517?casa_token=cEhJNO9eKEQAAAAA:v5XKej71f1QtR_Ugg0izKPmj_E18GRio0N6bcawszdJhw0f2_Rpk1BM8706-2GZO1cDjPLYzzajJhg> by Neil Gilbert a few years ago, and similar concepts are discussed in recent literature <https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/rse2.70027>.

Jeff
